params.question: A hordeolum internum differs from a hordeolum externum because it arises from infection of which structure?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Glands of Zeis are sebaceous glands at the lash base. Their infection produces hordeolum externum (the common stye), which points toward the skin.
Correct. Hordeolum internum infects the meibomian glands embedded within the tarsal plate, so the swelling points toward the palpebral conjunctiva rather than the skin.
Glands of Moll are modified sweat glands at the lid margin. Like Zeis glands, their infection produces hordeolum externum, not internum.
The lacrimal gland sits in the superolateral orbit and produces tears. Its infection is dacryoadenitis, an entirely separate condition from hordeolum.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. The gland determines the type: Zeis and Moll glands at the lash base → hordeolum externum (points to skin); meibomian glands within the tarsus → hordeolum internum (points to palpebral conjunctiva). Both are treated with warm compresses.

Correct. The meibomian glands lie deep within the tarsus, so hordeolum internum points toward the conjunctival surface — the key distinction from hordeolum externum, which involves Zeis or Moll glands and points toward the skin.

interactions.label: A child with sinusitis develops a swollen, red, tender eyelid. Which combination

params.question: A child with sinusitis develops a swollen, red, tender eyelid. Which combination of additional findings indicates that infection has crossed the orbital septum?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Systemic inflammatory markers may be raised in both preseptal and orbital cellulitis. They cannot localise infection relative to the orbital septum.

answers.text: Purulent discharge and crusting at the lash base

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Discharge and crusting suggest blepharitis or conjunctivitis, not postseptal spread. These findings do not reflect the position of infection relative to the septum.

answers.text: Proptosis, restricted painful eye movements, and reduced visual acuity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. These are the three danger signs of orbital cellulitis, confirming infection posterior to the septum within the closed bony orbit.
Contralateral lid oedema can occur with preseptal cellulitis from frontal sinusitis. It does not by itself confirm postseptal involvement.

overallFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. The orbital septum divides outpatient from emergency management. Three danger signs indicate infection has crossed it: proptosis, restricted and painful eye movements, and reduced visual acuity or an afferent pupillary defect. Any single one mandates IV antibiotics and urgent CT.

Correct. Proptosis, restricted painful eye movements, and reduced visual acuity are the three danger signs confirming postseptal infection. Any one of these mandates urgent IV antibiotics and CT imaging of the orbits.

interactions.label: In cavernous sinus thrombosis, cranial nerve III is the first nerve affected bec

params.question: In cavernous sinus thrombosis, cranial nerve III is the first nerve affected because it is the largest cranial nerve within the cavernous sinus.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is actually false. CN VI is the first nerve affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis. The reason is anatomical position: CN VI traverses the lumen of the sinus itself, in direct contact with infected venous blood, while the other nerves (III, IV, V1, V2) are relatively protected within the lateral wall.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Cranial nerve VI, not III, is the first affected. CN VI passes through the lumen of the cavernous sinus in direct contact with venous blood, while CN III, IV, V1, and V2 travel within the lateral wall. Its position, not its size, determines vulnerability.

params.question: A 35-year-old woman with Graves' disease presents with bilateral proptosis, lid retraction, and active thyroid eye disease. Vision and colour vision are normal. What is the most appropriate management?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Selenium is reserved for mild active thyroid eye disease. Bilateral proptosis with lid retraction represents moderate-to-severe active disease requiring more aggressive immunosuppression.

Correct. Bilateral proptosis with lid retraction in active disease with preserved vision indicates moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease, for which IV methylprednisolone pulses are the standard of care.
Urgent decompression is reserved for sight-threatening complications — compressive optic neuropathy or severe exposure keratopathy. Vision is normal in this patient.

answers.text: Rehabilitative lid surgery to correct the retraction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rehabilitative surgery (decompression → squint → lid, in that sequence) must wait until the disease has been inactive for three to six months. Operating during active disease risks worsening.

overallFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. The management ladder is: mild active → selenium; moderate-to-severe active (bilateral proptosis, lid retraction, preserved vision) → IV methylprednisolone pulses; sight-threatening (optic neuropathy or exposure keratopathy) → urgent orbital decompression. Rehabilitative surgery waits until 3–6 months of inactivity.

Correct. This patient has moderate-to-severe active thyroid eye disease without sight-threatening complications. IV methylprednisolone is the appropriate treatment. Rehabilitative surgery follows the fixed sequence of decompression, squint, then lid — only after 3–6 months of inactivity.

interactions.label: Which of the following presentations demands same-day ophthalmology referral?

params.question: Which of the following presentations demands same-day ophthalmology referral?

answers.text: A 2-year-old with a bluish lid mass that enlarges with crying

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes capillary haemangioma, the commonest vascular orbital tumour of infancy. It characteristically regresses spontaneously by age seven and does not require emergency referral.

answers.text: An adult with slowly progressive axial proptosis over two years

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Slow axial proptosis over years suggests cavernous haemangioma, a benign tumour. It requires evaluation, but the two-year tempo indicates a non-urgent process.

answers.text: A 5-year-old with rapidly progressive proptosis over three weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Rapidly progressive proptosis in a child is rhabdomyosarcoma until proven otherwise — the commonest primary orbital malignancy of childhood. This is an oncological emergency demanding urgent biopsy.

answers.text: An adult with stable, painless proptosis and an S-shaped upper lid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This pattern suggests pleomorphic adenoma of the lacrimal gland. While en-bloc excision without capsule breach is essential, the stable tempo does not mandate same-day referral.

overallFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. Four red flags demand same-day referral: rapidly progressive proptosis in a child (rhabdomyosarcoma), any proptosis with declining vision or colour desaturation, bilateral orbital signs evolving in hours (cavernous sinus thrombosis), and orbital cellulitis not improving after 48 hours of IV antibiotics.

Correct. Rapidly progressive proptosis in a child is one of four red flags for same-day referral. The others are: proptosis with declining vision or colour desaturation, bilateral orbital signs evolving in hours (cavernous sinus thrombosis), and orbital cellulitis not improving after 48 hours of IV antibiotics.
